headline: Everybody's Drifting Sloop Channel for Fluke — I'm Working the Inlet Rip at Dusk
subhead: The doormats are there for the boat guys, but the real money right now is on the moving current and the after-dark bass sliding into the rocks.
body_markdown:
Every guy I talked to at the ramp this week wanted to tell me about the fluke bite in the bay — Sloop Channel, the flats off Short Beach, everybody drifting Gulp and bucktails like it's the only game in town. And look, I get it, the fluke are there and they're feeding good on the moving tide. But I'm not a bay guy in August. I'm an inlet guy, and right now the inlet is where the real story is, especially once the sun starts dropping.

Here's the thing nobody wants to talk about in July and August — the ocean side of Jones Beach has been rough, sloppy, three-foot swell rolling in on a short period, and that junk water pushes everything with fins into the channels and the structure where it's calm. That's exactly what's happening at Jones Inlet right now. Water on the ocean side is sitting warm, mid-70s, maybe pushing higher on the surface, and that heat combined with the chop has the bass doing what they do every summer — holding deep on structure all day, then coming up hard at first light and again at dusk and through the night to hit bait.

I've been working the rocks at the inlet on the last two hours of the outgoing and into the start of the incoming, right at last light. That current edge where the deep water meets the shallow flat on the west side of the inlet — that's holding bass in the 26 to 34 inch range, mixed slot fish with a few overslots mixed in, and they're eating eels. Not artificial eels, live eels, snap them on a fishfinder rig or just a plain hook through the lips and let the current do the work. Bunker chunks are working too if you can't get eels, fished on the bottom in that same seam. The bite window is tight — maybe 45 minutes on either side of last light, then again a couple hours before dawn if you've got the stomach for it.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the current would stay strong into early August and that's the window to fish hard water before the tides go soft, and that's exactly what's playing out. The moon's sliding toward that first-quarter neap around the 5th and 6th, and once that hits, the current through the inlet is going to lose some teeth. Right now though, we've still got good push on the tide, and that's pulling bait through the rip and stacking bass right behind it. I wouldn't waste this week's strong water — once the neap sets in, you're going to need to fish the absolute peak of the current to get bit, probably down at the Wantagh Bridge pilings or deeper holes where the current concentrates even when the range is small.

Bluefish are doing their thing just outside the inlet mouth, and this is where the boat guys have an edge on us jetty rats — bunker pods are holding tight to the beach on the ocean side after getting pushed around by the swell, and wherever those pods sit, the blues find them fast. If you see birds working tight over the water just off Jones Beach, that's your signal, run there and throw poppers or just troll umbrella rigs through the edge of the bait. From the beach, if a pod pushes in close to the bar, you can connect with bucktails and metal, but you need to be in the right spot at the right time — it's not a sure thing casting blind.

Fluke, fine, I'll give the bay its due. Sloop Channel and the flats around Short Beach are holding decent numbers on the last of the incoming into the top of the tide, fish in the 18 to 22 inch class on white Gulp Swimming Mullets rigged on 3/4 ounce bucktails, working depths of 12 to 20 feet where the channel bends. If you want a doormat, drift the deeper cuts near the inlet mouth itself where the current really rips — that's where the bigger fish sit waiting on bait getting swept through. But I'm telling you, once that sun gets low, I'm reeling in the fluke rod and picking up the eel outfit.

Weakfish are still a bonus fish more than a target right now, but I've heard of a few being picked up in the bay on light jigs during the same tide stages as the fluke — worth a look if you're already out there, don't build a whole trip around it yet.

Looking ahead, the next few days should still fish well on the inlet structure while we've got strong tidal push, but that neap coming in around the 5th and 6th is going to soften things up fast. When that happens, I'd shift my effort to the deepest, coolest water I can find at the peak of whatever current is left — the Wantagh Bridge at night, the deepest bends in the inlet channel, anywhere the water still moves with authority. If the bunker stay tight to the ocean beach like they have been, keep an eye on the birds — that blitz can fire off with almost no warning, and when it does, you want to already be rigged and ready, not scrambling for tackle in the truck.
